sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to Simulator 7.2 Tab A. Here we simulate classical errors-in-variables. When physical sensor noise corrupts predictor X-star equals X plus u, Ordinary Least Squares slope collapses by the reliability ratio lambda equals sigma-X squared over sigma-X squared plus sigma-u squared. Adjust the noise sliders to see Group zero's slope collapse while Group one remains sharp.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Look at the orange line for Group zero, Dr. Nova! It is almost completely flat! The true underlying relationship between X and Y is identical for both groups, but the noisy sensor makes Group zero look completely unresponsive!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Time for Active Checkpoint 1. In a simple linear regression Y equals beta X plus epsilon, suppose X is measured through a noisy sensor X-star equals X plus u, where noise u is independent of X and disturbance epsilon. What is the probability limit of the OLS slope estimator beta-hat?

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Dr. Nova, this is the exact proof we derived earlier using covariance expansion. Let's test whether our learners can identify the asymptotic OLS slope under zero-mean independent sensor noise!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Outstanding! That is correct. Expanding the covariance reveals Covariance of X-star and Y equals beta sigma-X squared, while the variance of X-star equals sigma-X squared plus sigma-u squared. Their ratio yields the reliability ratio lambda-rel, strictly attenuating the estimated slope toward zero.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Not quite. Remember that independent measurement noise adds uninformative variance into the denominator of the OLS estimator, while leaving numerator covariance unchanged. This strictly dilutes the estimated slope toward zero by the factor sigma-X squared over sigma-X squared plus sigma-u squared.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to Interactive Lab 2: Simulator 7.2 Tab B. Here, you can directly manipulate subgroup slope and centroid offsets to trigger Simpson's Paradox. Adjust the centroid offsets to watch the global pooled dashed red line flip from positive to negative, even though both subgroups remain positive!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Dr. Nova, this is amazing! Both groups clearly point upwards, but the global line slants downwards! If we deployed this model, an applicant who increases their score would actually get a lower probability of approval!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Let us test your understanding in Active Checkpoint 2. In the famous 1975 UC Berkeley graduate admissions audit, aggregate university statistics showed male applicants were admitted at 44% compared to 35% for female applicants. Yet within individual departments, female applicants were admitted at equal or higher rates! What statistical phenomenon caused this reversal?

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: This is one of the most famous real-world paradoxes in statistics history, Dr. Nova! Let's see if our learners can distinguish between department-level confounding and overt institutional bias.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Correct! Female applicants disproportionately applied to highly competitive departments with low overall admission rates, such as English and History, while male applicants applied to engineering and science departments with higher baseline admission rates. Conditioning on department eliminated the aggregate disparity.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Incorrect. The aggregate reversal was not caused by test scores or database errors. It was caused by confounding: female applicants applied in greater numbers to departments that were extremely selective for all applicants, pulling down their overall pooled acceptance rate.
